input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.

Topic: CSCI-636: Information Retrieval. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: An introduction to the theories and techniques used to construct search engines. Topics include search interfaces, traditional retrieval models (e.g., TF-IDF, BM25), modern retrieval techniques (e.g., neural reranking and retrieval), search engine evaluation, and search applications (e.g., conversational IR, enterprise search). Students will also review current IR research, provide written summaries of current research papers, and complete a group project in which they will design and execute experiments for search engine components. Prerequisites:(CSCI-603 and CSCI-605 and CSCI-661 with grades of B or better, including familiarity with computer science concepts) or CSCI-331 or equivalent courses. Students may not take and receive credit for both CSCI-636 and CSCI-536. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring

Source excerpts:

[nist-ai-rmf]
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organizes work around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. Govern establishes policies, responsibilities, and accountability for AI risk. Map documents context, intended use, affected people, and potential impacts. Measure uses qualitative and quantitative methods to analyze identified risks. Manage prioritizes risks and allocates resources for response and monitoring. Risk analysis considers data quality and uncertainty. It also considers robustness, privacy, security, transparency, and fairness. Monitoring continues after deployment because context and system behavior can change.

[rit-csci-636]
An introduction to the theories and techniques used to construct search engines. Topics include search interfaces, traditional retrieval models (e.g., TF-IDF, BM25), modern retrieval techniques (e.g., neural reranking and retrieval), search engine evaluation, and search applications (e.g., conversational IR, enterprise search). Students will also review current IR research, provide written summaries of current research papers, and complete a group project in which they will design and execute experiments for search engine components. Prerequisites:(CSCI-603 and CSCI-605 and CSCI-661 with grades of B or better, including familiarity with computer science concepts) or CSCI-331 or equivalent courses. Students may not take and receive credit for both CSCI-636 and CSCI-536. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring

[scikit-learn-user-guide]
Machine-learning workflows separate data preparation, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation. Supervised methods learn a mapping from examples paired with target labels. Unsupervised methods identify structure without target labels. Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage. Pipelines combine preprocessing and estimators so the same transformations are applied consistently. Cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined data splits. Evaluation metrics must match the task and the cost of different errors. Hyperparameter selection must remain separate from final test evaluation. Leakage, distribution shift, overfitting, and unexamined assumptions can invalidate results.

beats.claim: Search engines rely on a structured pipeline that transforms user queries into ranked document results through indexing, retrieval, and ranking stages.
beats.example: A user types 'machine learning basics' into a search bar, and the system returns a ranked list of documents matching the query terms.
beats.title: Introduction to Search Engine Architecture
beats.visualDirection: Display a horizontal flowchart with three labeled boxes: Query Input, Index/Retrieval, and Ranked Results, connected by arrows indicating data flow.

beats.claim: Raw user queries undergo tokenization, stop-word removal, and stemming or lemmatization to normalize text before matching against the document index.
beats.example: The query 'running shoes' is tokenized into ['running', 'shoes'], with 'running' stemmed to 'run' to match variations like 'runs' or 'ran'.
beats.title: Query Processing and Preprocessing
beats.visualDirection: Show a split-screen graphic: left side shows raw query text, right side shows processed tokens with arrows indicating preprocessing steps.

beats.claim: The Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) model ranks documents by calculating the product of a term's frequency within a document and its inverse frequency across the
beats.example: A term appearing frequently in one document but rarely across the corpus receives a high TF-IDF score, boosting its ranking position.
beats.title: Traditional Retrieval: TF-IDF
beats.visualDirection: Render a bar chart comparing TF-IDF scores for three terms across two documents, highlighting the inverse document frequency component.

beats.claim: The BM25 algorithm refines TF-IDF by incorporating position weighting, query length normalization, and a saturation function to reduce the impact of overly frequent terms.
beats.example: A term appearing at the beginning of a document receives a higher position weight, while the saturation function prevents rare terms from dominating the score.
beats.title: Traditional Retrieval: BM25
beats.visualDirection: Display a formula breakdown with labeled components: position weight, query length normalization, and saturation function, alongside a sample score calculation.

beats.claim: Neural reranking models use deep learning architectures to re-score initially retrieved documents by learning complex semantic relationships between queries and passages.
beats.example: A transformer-based reranker reorders a top-100 list of documents by analyzing contextual embeddings, promoting documents with higher semantic alignment.
beats.title: Modern Retrieval: Neural Reranking
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a two-stage pipeline: first stage shows traditional retrieval output, second stage shows neural reranker adjusting document order with attention visualization.

beats.claim: Dense retrieval techniques map queries and documents into a shared vector space using neural encoders, enabling similarity search through cosine distance calculations.
beats.example: A query and a document are encoded into 768-dimensional vectors, and the system retrieves the top-k documents with the smallest cosine distance to the query vector.
beats.title: Modern Retrieval: Dense Retrieval
beats.visualDirection: Show a 2D projection of query and document vectors with distance metrics, emphasizing the shared embedding space and cosine similarity calculation.

beats.claim: Search performance is evaluated using metrics like precision, recall, mean average precision (MAP), and nDCG, which measure relevance and ranking quality across result sets.
beats.example: MAP calculates the average precision at the top of the ranked list, providing a single score that reflects overall ranking effectiveness.
beats.title: Search Engine Evaluation Metrics
beats.visualDirection: Present a table comparing precision, recall, MAP, and nDCG with brief definitions and a sample calculation for MAP.

beats.claim: Conversational information retrieval systems maintain dialogue state across multiple turns, using context-aware retrieval to answer follow-up questions accurately.
beats.example: After a user asks 'What is NLP?', the system retrieves relevant documents and uses the context to answer 'How does NLP work?' in the next turn.
beats.title: Search Applications: Conversational IR
beats.visualDirection: Display a dialogue flow with user queries and system responses, highlighting context tracking and retrieval steps at each turn.

beats.claim: Enterprise search systems integrate with organizational data sources, enforce access controls, and support faceted navigation to help users find internal documents efficiently.
beats.example: An employee searches for 'Q3 financial report' and filters results by department, date range, and document type to locate the correct internal document.
beats.title: Search Applications: Enterprise Search
beats.visualDirection: Show a dashboard with search bar, filter panel, and results list, emphasizing access controls and faceted navigation features.

beats.claim: Designing experiments for search components requires defining a baseline, selecting a test corpus, controlling variables, and evaluating performance using standardized metrics.
beats.example: Compare a TF-IDF baseline against a BM25 model on a news corpus, measuring MAP and nDCG to determine which ranking algorithm performs better.
beats.title: Experimental Design for Retrieval Components
beats.visualDirection: Create a comparison table with columns for Baseline, Model, Corpus, Metrics, and Results, highlighting controlled experimental variables.
